summary: Defines a Sieve extension that adds a test for whether a special-use attribute is assigned to a mailbox, based on the IMAP SPECIAL-USE capability from RFC 6154. It also lets a filter deliver mail into a mailbox identified by its special use. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Email filters can find the folder called 'Junk' or 'Sent' by its job instead of its name, even when it is named differently in another language.

questions: deliver to junk folder with sieve
how to file mail into the junk folder with sieve
subtitle: Lets a Sieve mail filter file messages into the Junk, Sent or Archive folder by its job rather than its name.

tldr.problem: IMAP clients can find special-use mailboxes such as drafts, sent or spam by attribute, but the Sieve filtering language had no way to do the same.
tldr.mechanism: The "special-use" extension adds a specialuse_exists test and a :specialuse argument to fileinto, so a script can name a mailbox by its special-use attribute and fall back to a default mailbox name.
tldr.outcome: Scripts can deliver to the user's Junk or Archive mailbox without knowing what it is called, and without needing the IMAP METADATA capability.

today: RFC 8579 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2019. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why Sieve Needs Special-Use Mailboxes
sections.content:
Many IMAP mailboxes have a special use, such as holding drafts, copies of sent messages, or spam. The IMAP SPECIAL-USE capability (RFC 6154) gives these mailboxes attributes so a client can find them without guessing names. That simplifies client configuration.

The Sieve mail filtering language (RFC 5228) had no such access. A Sieve script could not, for example, find the user's spam mailbox at delivery. Limited access existed through the "mboxmetadata" extension (RFC 5490), but that needs the IMAP METADATA capability, which not every implementer wants to add just for this.
sections.eli5: Your mail app knows which folder is the Junk folder, but the mail sorting robot did not. This memo teaches the robot to find folders by their job.

sections.title: The specialuse_exists Test
sections.content:
The new test has the form specialuse_exists [<mailbox>] <special-use-attrs>. Without a mailbox argument, it is true when, for every listed attribute, at least one mailbox in the user's personal namespace has that attribute and allows the user to deliver messages into it.

With a mailbox argument, it is true when that mailbox exists, allows delivery, and has all of the listed attributes assigned. The definition of when delivery is possible comes from the "mailboxexists" test in RFC 5490.

The RFC also shows the equivalent IMAP steps: a NAMESPACE command, an extended LIST with SPECIAL-USE, and MYRIGHTS to confirm the user has insert rights.
sections.eli5: The test asks: is there a folder that does this job, and may I put mail in it? If yes, the answer is true.

sections.title: The :specialuse Argument to fileinto
sections.content:
The fileinto command gains an optional :specialuse argument: fileinto [:specialuse <special-use-attr>] <mailbox>. If a mailbox in the user's personal namespace has that attribute, the message goes there. Otherwise, or if the attribute is unknown to the implementation, fileinto behaves as it would without the argument and uses the named default mailbox.

If several mailboxes have the attribute and one of them is the default mailbox, that one MUST be used. If not, the choice is implementation defined, but implementations SHOULD choose consistently while the attribute assignments are unchanged.

If delivery to the special-use mailbox fails for reasons other than its not existing, the interpreter MUST NOT fall back to the default mailbox. This prevents messages from being spread over two mailboxes after a transient failure.

The attribute string may contain variables when the "variables" extension is active, in which case its syntax is checked only at runtime.
sections.eli5: The filter first looks for the folder with the right job. If there is none, it uses the folder name you gave it. If the right folder is there but broken, it does not switch to the backup, so your mail never gets split up.

sections.title: Implicit Creation of Mailboxes
sections.content:
The fileinto command may implicitly create a missing mailbox, and the "mailbox" extension's :create argument can request this explicitly. With :specialuse this does not change: if neither the special-use mailbox nor the default mailbox is found, the default mailbox is created if needed.

If the server supports the CREATE-SPECIAL-USE capability, it SHOULD assign the requested special-use attribute to the newly created mailbox.
sections.eli5: If neither folder exists, the filter makes the one you named and, if it can, gives it the right job label.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The first example files mail into the mailbox with the \Junk attribute, and if none exists, into a mailbox named "Spam". If "Spam" does not exist either, the result is implementation dependent.

The second example adds the "mailbox" extension and :create, so "Spam" is created when neither mailbox exists, and the \Junk attribute may be assigned to it.

The third example runs from an IMAP event (RFC 6785) rather than at delivery. It redirects a message to an automated recipient when it is copied into a mailbox that has the \Junk attribute, using specialuse_exists with a variable holding the mailbox name.
sections.eli5: One example says: put it in the Junk-job folder, or in a folder called Spam if there is none. Another one sends a copy to a spam-checking helper when you drop mail into the Junk folder.

sections.title: Security and Scope Limits
sections.content:
The RFC believes the extension adds no new security concerns beyond those of Sieve, the variables extension and SPECIAL-USE. It does deliberately restrict the special-use mailbox to the user's personal namespace.

There are two reasons. Searching all mail storage for a particular attribute could put undue load on the system, and shared special-use mailboxes are deemed of limited use with the currently defined attributes. It also prevents messages from being unexpectedly or even maliciously filed into shared mailboxes whose attributes apply to all users. The restriction could be lifted for future attributes with a clear shared use, after careful consideration of the security concerns.
sections.eli5: The filter only looks in your own folders, never in folders shared with other people, so your mail cannot be sent somewhere surprising.

sections.title: Capability String and IANA
sections.content: An implementation that provides the test and the argument advertises the Sieve capability string special-use, and scripts load it with require "special-use". IANA registered the extension in the Sieve Extensions registry, with the Sieve discussion list as the contact address.
sections.eli5: Each Sieve add-on has a name tag. This one is called special-use, and scripts say its name to switch it on.
